title: Balance
lead: Why a drink tastes right, and how to fix one that doesn’t.

sections.name: Core, balance, seasoning

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Every drink has a core, something that balances it, and a seasoning.

know: The core is the main flavor, usually the spirit.
Balance makes the core easier to drink: sugar, acid or both.
Seasoning adds depth: bitters, a rinse, the garnish.
sections.source: Cocktail Codex (Alex Day, Nick Fauchald and David Kaplan, Ten Speed Press, 2018), as summarized by the publisher (randomhousebooks.com) and reviews

sections.name: Strong, sweet, sour

lines.label: In short
lines.text: A sour is strong, sweet and sour in proportion.

know: A common starting point is 2 parts spirit to ¾ sour to 1 sweet.
That ratio comes out sweet, not sour, with rich syrup.
Start there, then taste and move one thing.

sections.name: Syrup strength

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Rich syrup and simple syrup aren’t swapped one for one.

know: Simple is 1:1 sugar to water; rich is 2:1.
Rich is about 1.35× as sweet, not twice.
To swap rich for simple, use about 1½ times as much simple.
sections.source: Difford’s Guide, “2 to 1 ‘rich’ sugar syrup versus 1 to 1 ‘simple’ syrup” (diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/3593)

sections.name: Taste and adjust

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Taste every drink you build before it leaves.

know: Taste with a straw, never from the tin.
Too sharp: a touch more sweet. Too sweet: a touch more citrus.
Change one thing at a time.

keyPoints.line: is the main flavor, usually the spirit.

read.bigIdea: Every drink is a core, a balance and a seasoning.
read.where: Cocktail Codex breaks every drink into three parts. The **core** is the main flavor: in an Old Fashioned, the **whiskey**. The **balance** makes the core easier to drink: there, the **sugar**. The **seasoning** adds depth: the **bitters**. Name the three parts of any drink and you can fix it, or build a new one.
read.mixup: The **garnish** isn’t decoration. A peel’s oils are seasoning, and they change the taste.
read.sayIt: It’s whiskey, softened with a little sugar and seasoned with bitters.

video.title: Understanding The 2:1:1 Cocktail Formula for Sours - Course 2 Lesson 05

keyPoints.line: spirit, sour, sweet: a common starting point.
with rich syrup. Most bars pull the sugar back.

read.bigIdea: A sour is three things in proportion.
read.where: Every sour has a **strong** part (the spirit), a **sour** part (citrus) and a **sweet** part (syrup or liqueur). A common “golden ratio” is **2 parts spirit, ¾ sour, 1 sweet**. Difford’s Guide points out it comes out **sweet rather than sour**, especially with **rich syrup**, so many bars cut the sugar or add citrus. Our specs are where we’ve landed: start there.
read.mixup: A ratio is a **starting point**, not a rule. Every citrus and every syrup is a little different.
read.sayIt: Would you like it on the tart side or a little sweeter?

video.title: Essential Cocktail Syrups | Sugars in cocktails EXPLAINED, Vol.1

keyPoints.line: simple syrup: sugar and water, equal parts.
swap rich for simple with about half as much again.

read.bigIdea: Know which syrup a spec means.
read.where: **Simple syrup** is **1:1** sugar to water. **Rich syrup** is **2:1**. Rich isn’t twice as sweet: Difford’s Guide measures it at about **1.35 times**. So to swap rich for simple, use about **1½ times** as much simple (10 ml rich ≈ 15 ml simple). Simple also adds more water to the drink, about **5–8%** more dilution.
read.mixup: Doubling the simple to replace rich makes the drink **too sweet and too watery**.

video.title: The Secret to Perfectly Balanced Cocktails

keyPoints.line: taste every drink, never from the tin.
a touch more citrus, or a dash of bitters.

read.bigIdea: Taste before it leaves the bar.
read.where: Dip a **straw**, cap it with a finger, taste. If it’s **too sharp**, it wants a little more sweet. If it’s **too sweet** or flat, a little more **citrus** or a **dash of bitters**. If it’s **hot** with alcohol, it may need more dilution: shake or stir longer. Change **one thing at a time**, so you know what fixed it.
read.mixup: Changing two things at once means you never learn which one worked.

sources: Cocktail Codex (Alex Day, Nick Fauchald and David Kaplan, Ten Speed Press, 2018), as summarized by the publisher (randomhousebooks.com) and reviews; Difford’s Guide, Whiskey Sour (diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2083); Difford’s Guide, “2 to 1 ‘rich’ sugar syrup versus 1 to 1 ‘simple’ syrup” (diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/3593). Checked Nov 8, 2026.
